daily_brief: The day's headlines are dominated by violence, political upheaval, and diplomatic signaling. Two mass shootings in South Africa killed 28 people near Johannesburg and Cape Town, underscoring the country's ongoing struggle with violent crime [BBC, Guardian, Globe and Mail]. In Europe, Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić formally resigned after months of student-led protests over corruption, paving the way for early elections in which he will seek the prime ministership [BBC]. Pope Leo XIV concluded his four-day visit to France with a speech in Metz invoking Robert Schuman's vision of European unity, warning against 'lies and deceit' in international relations and calling for peace negotiations—an apparent reference to the war in Ukraine [RFI, France 24, BBC]. Switzerland overwhelmingly rejected a referendum that would have imposed stricter neutrality rules, signaling continued support for EU sanctions against Russia [BBC]. Meanwhile, fighting has intensified in northern Ethiopia, with the TPLF launching offensives and Addis Ababa accusing Sudan and Egypt of backing rebel forces [Guardian, Al Jazeera]. On migration, three people including a child died attempting a Channel crossing from France to the UK, bringing this year's toll to 20 [BBC, Le Monde].

top_stories.headline: Two Mass Shootings in South Africa Kill 28 Near Johannesburg and Cape Town
bullets: Eight gunmen armed with AK-47s stormed a bar in Wedela township near Johannesburg on Saturday night, killing 18 people and wounding at least 14; attackers also set vehicles on fire and took personal belongings.
A separate shooting hours later at an entertainment venue in Lwandle township near Cape Town killed 10 people and wounded 11.
Police have not confirmed motives but are investigating links to robbery and possible turf wars between illegal mining groups; no arrests have been made.
President Cyril Ramaphosa called the violence unacceptable and pledged to reduce criminality amid ongoing scrutiny of police corruption.

top_stories.headline: Serbian President Vučić Resigns After Year of Protests, Eyes Prime Ministership
bullets: Aleksandar Vučić formally resigned as Serbia's president on Monday after more than a year of student-led protests over alleged government corruption.
Protests intensified following the 2024 collapse of Novi Sad railway station roof that killed 16 people, which demonstrators linked to systemic mismanagement.
Vučić, who cannot seek a third presidential term, is standing as his party's candidate for prime minister in upcoming parliamentary elections.
His resignation triggers early elections; he addressed supporters claiming his administration preserved peace and stability.

sources.name: BBC Europe
sources.framing_note: Neutral account emphasizing protest origins and constitutional constraints.

top_stories.headline: Pope Leo XIV Concludes France Visit with Call for European Unity and Peace
bullets: Pope Leo XIV delivered a speech in Metz on the final day of his four-day France visit, invoking EU founding father Robert Schuman's vision of peace through cooperation.
He warned that relations between nations were becoming 'increasingly uncivilised' and urged 'courage in negotiation' for peace—an apparent reference to Ukraine.
Earlier in Lourdes, the Pope met with seven survivors of clergy abuse and called on French bishops to root out the 'scourge' of sexual abuse.
A 2021 inquiry found clergy or Church members had abused approximately 330,000 children in France over 70 years.

top_stories.headline: Switzerland Overwhelmingly Rejects Stricter Neutrality Referendum
bullets: Over 70% of Swiss voters rejected a proposal that would have prevented Switzerland from imposing sanctions without UN approval.
The initiative, backed by the right-wing Swiss People's Party and openly supported by Russia, would also have blocked closer ties with NATO.
The federal government and all other major parties opposed the measure.
Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis stated neutrality 'does not mean indifference' and Switzerland would not ignore violations of international rules.

sources.name: BBC Europe
sources.framing_note: Straightforward coverage noting Moscow's backing of the initiative.

top_stories.headline: Fighting Intensifies in Northern Ethiopia as Government Accuses Sudan, Egypt of Backing Rebels
bullets: The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) launched attacks into Afar and Amhara regions and seized three airports from federal police.
Ethiopian Airlines suspended flights to Tigray and the historic town of Lalibela due to nearby fighting.
Ethiopia's army commander accused Sudan and Egypt of backing the rebel alliance; Sudan denied the claims and counter-accused Ethiopia of supporting the RSF.
Seven armed groups, including the TPLF, announced formation of the Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival aimed at overthrowing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government.

sources.name: The Guardian
sources.framing_note: Provided historical context on 2020-2022 war deaths and civilian fears of siege conditions.

sources.framing_note: Emphasized mutual accusations between Ethiopia and Sudan regarding proxy support.

additional_stories.headline: Three people, including a 10-year-old child, died attempting to cross the English Channel from France when their overcrowded boat got into difficulty.
Swedish Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson says she cannot form a government despite her bloc's narrow election victory after a coalition partner defected on a key vote.
Hurricane Polo, a Category 3 storm, is expected to make landfall on Mexico's Baja California peninsula with life-threatening flooding and mudslides forecast.
Five UK nationals were arrested near RAF Fairford, a US-operated air base in England, on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act; police are investigating possible links to Iran.
Bangkok was declared a disaster zone after nearly 300mm of rain fell in 48 hours, killing at least eight people and causing an estimated $466 million in damage.
A German town near Dresden voted to ban 'stumbling stone' Holocaust memorials from public spaces, drawing criticism from Germany's education minister.
Australian Greens leader Larissa Waters stepped down due to a chronic kidney condition after 16 months in the role.
France's far-right National Rally secured a record 14 seats in Senate elections, with Marine Le Pen hailing the result as a 'victory.'
Israeli football fans directed monkey chants at Ireland's Adam Idah and chanted military slogans during a Nations League match, but faced no UEFA disciplinary action.
